data.label: **React** · the library for web and native user interfaces

data.text: Created by **Jordan Walke** at Facebook and open-sourced in **2013**. You describe the UI as a function of state, and React works out how to update the screen. Latest version: **19.3.1** (October 2026). Since February 2026 React is governed by the **React Foundation**, part of the Linux Foundation.

**How to read this map**
The number on a topic means there is more inside: click it to open. Code is shown as monospace lines. Links go to the official docs at react.dev.
Components, JSX, props, state, events, lists, context, refs.
Every built-in hook, the rules, and custom hooks.
Render and commit, reconciliation, Fiber, scheduling, the compiler.
Gotchas with effects, state, rendering and the server.
Every major version from 2011 to 19.3, and what changed.
Composition, state management, memoization, profiling.
SSR, Server Components, Server Functions, Next.js, Vite.
Questions, "what does this log?" puzzles, live coding.
From "React in 100 seconds" to the talks that introduced Fiber and Hooks.

data.label: A Complete Guide to useEffect — Dan Abramov

data.text: A component is a **function that returns UI**. Names start with a capital letter, so React can tell `<Card />` from the `<div>` tag. Components can be nested and reused like building blocks.

HTML-like syntax that compiles to function calls (`jsx()`, formerly `React.createElement`). Put any JavaScript expression in **curly braces**. Attributes are camelCase: `className`, `onClick`, `htmlFor`. A component returns **one root**; use a Fragment `<>…</>` to group.

Props are a component's **inputs**, passed like HTML attributes and received as one object. They are **read-only**: a component must never change its own props. Anything can be a prop: strings, objects, functions, other elements.

State is a component's **memory**. Calling the setter schedules a **re-render** with the new value. Each render sees a fixed **snapshot** of state, so the variable doesn't change until the next render.

Rendering must be a **pure calculation**: same props and state, same JSX. No side effects during render: no fetching, no subscriptions, no changing variables outside the component. Side effects belong in **event handlers** or, as a last resort, **effects**.
Pass a **function** to `onClick`, don't call it. React passes a cross-browser **synthetic event**. Since React 17 listeners are attached to the root container, not to `document`.

```jsx
// Right: pass a function
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
<button onClick={() => remove(id)}>Delete</button>

// Wrong: calls it during render
<button onClick={remove(id)}>Delete</button>
```
Use plain JavaScript: `if`, the ternary `? :` and `&&`. Returning `null` renders nothing. Beware `count && <List />`: when `count` is `0`, React renders a **0**.

Render lists with `map`. Each item needs a **key** that is stable and unique among siblings, usually an id from the data. Keys tell React which item is which between renders; avoid the array index if items can move.

```jsx
    {todos.map((todo) => (
  • {todo.text}
    • ))}
```
Nesting JSX passes it as the **children** prop. Composition replaces inheritance in React: wrapper components accept children, or take elements in named props as "slots".
Data flows **down** through props; changes flow **up** through callbacks. When two components need the same state, **lift it up** to their closest common parent and pass it down.

A **controlled** input gets its value from state and reports changes with `onChange`: React state is the single source of truth. An **uncontrolled** input keeps its own value in the DOM and is read with a ref or from the form on submit.
Context passes a value to the **whole subtree** without threading props through every level: themes, the signed-in user, locale. Since React 19, `<ThemeContext>` itself is the provider.

A ref holds a value that **survives renders without causing them**: a DOM node, a timer id, the previous value. Changing `ref.current` doesn't re-render. Since React 19, function components receive `ref` as a normal prop.

Effects **synchronise** a component with something outside React: a network connection, a browser API, a third-party widget. They run after the screen updates. If no external system is involved, you probably **don't need an effect**.

data.text:
1. Break the UI into a component hierarchy
2. Build a static version with props only
3. Find the **minimal** state; derive everything else
4. Decide which component owns each piece of state
5. Add inverse data flow with callbacks

data.label: **Hooks** · functions that let components use React features

data.text:
**Rules of Hooks**
- Call hooks only at the **top level** of a component or custom hook: never in loops, conditions or after an early return
- Call them only from **React functions**, not plain functions or classes
- `use()` is the exception: it can be called conditionally
Why: React matches each hook call to its stored state **by call order**.

`const [v, setV] = useState(initial)`
Local state. Pass a function to compute the initial value lazily, and an **updater** `setV(prev => …)` when the new value depends on the old one.

`const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, init)`
State changes described as **actions** handled in one pure function. Good when many updates touch the same state.

`const theme = useContext(ThemeContext)`
Reads the nearest provider's value and re-renders when it changes.

`const data = use(promise)` / `use(Context)`
Reads a **promise** (suspends until it resolves) or a context. Unlike other hooks, it may be called in conditions and loops.

`const ref = useRef(initial)`
A mutable box `{ current }` that persists across renders without re-rendering.
Customises what a parent gets through a ref: expose `focus()` instead of the whole DOM node.

`useEffect(setup, deps)`
Runs **after paint**. Re-runs when a dependency changes (compared with `Object.is`); the cleanup runs before the next run and on unmount.
Runs **before paint**, after the DOM is updated. For measuring layout (tooltip position). It blocks painting, so use it sparingly.
Runs before layout effects. Only for CSS-in-JS libraries that inject `<style>` tags.
Wraps a function used inside an effect so it always sees the **latest** props and state **without** being a dependency.

`const v = useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b])`
Caches a **calculated value** between renders.

`const fn = useCallback(() => …, [deps])`
Caches a **function** so its identity stays stable, e.g. for a `memo` child.

`const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()`
Marks an update as **non-urgent** so typing and clicks stay responsive.

`const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)`
A copy of a value that **lags behind** during heavy renders.

`const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState(fn, init)`
State that is updated by an **action**, such as a form submission, with a built-in pending flag.
Shows an **optimistic** value while an action runs, then switches back to the real one.
From `react-dom`. Inside a `<form>`, reads its `pending` status and submitted data: handy for submit buttons.
A unique id that **matches on server and client**, for `htmlFor` and ARIA attributes. Never use it for list keys.

`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot)`
Subscribes to a store outside React without **tearing**. Used by Redux, Zustand and others.
Adds a label to a custom hook in React DevTools.
Extract stateful logic into a function whose name starts with `use`. Each component that calls it gets its **own** state. Open for examples.
Returns a value that only updates after it stops changing for `delay` ms. Typical for search boxes.
State that is saved to `localStorage`. The lazy initialiser reads storage only once.
Fetches JSON and **aborts** the request when the URL changes or the component unmounts, so a slow old response can't overwrite a new one.
Remembers the value from the previous render. The effect runs after render, so during render the ref still holds the old value.
Subscribes to a browser API with `useSyncExternalStore`, the safe way to read external mutable data.
The smallest useful custom hook: a boolean with a stable toggle function.
A render starts on the **initial mount** (`createRoot().render()`) or when **state changes** (`setState`, a context value, a parent re-rendering).
React **calls your components** to get the new tree of elements. This is pure calculation and can be paused, restarted or thrown away.
React **diffs** the new tree against the previous one to find the minimal set of changes.
React applies the changes to the **DOM** in one go, attaches refs, then runs layout effects. This phase can't be interrupted.
The browser **paints**. Then React runs `useEffect` callbacks: cleanups first, then setups.

JSX creates plain objects: `{ type, props, key, ref }`. They are cheap descriptions of what should be on screen. React keeps the previous tree and compares it with the new one; the word "virtual DOM" is about this idea, the React team now rarely uses it.

A full tree diff is O(n³). React makes it O(n) with two assumptions:
1. Elements of a **different type** produce different trees: the old subtree is destroyed and its state lost
2. **Keys** identify children across renders
Same type at the same position: React keeps the component and its state and updates the props.

The engine since React 16. Each component instance is a **fiber**: a unit of work linked to its child, sibling and parent. Rendering walks this list in small steps, so it can **pause** and yield to the browser. Open for more.

Updates get a **priority** ("lane"): a click or keypress is urgent, a transition is not. In concurrent rendering React works in slices of about **5 ms** and checks whether the browser needs the main thread, so urgent updates can interrupt slow ones.

Several state updates in the same event are **batched** into one render. Since React 18 this also happens in promises, timeouts and native handlers (**automatic batching**). `flushSync` forces an update to apply immediately.

Each fiber stores its hooks as a **linked list** in call order. On every render React walks the list again: the 1st `useState` call gets the 1st slot, and so on. That is why hooks can't be called conditionally.

Since React 18, React can prepare several versions of the UI at once and **interrupt** a render that is no longer needed. You opt in through transitions, `useDeferredValue` and Suspense. Your code must be pure for this to be safe.

When a component isn't ready (lazy code, `use(promise)`, data in a framework), it **suspends**: React shows the nearest `<Suspense>` fallback and retries when the data arrives. On the server, boundaries let HTML **stream** in pieces.

With server rendering, the HTML arrives first; then React **hydrates** it: renders the same tree in the browser and attaches event handlers instead of recreating the DOM. Since 18, **selective hydration** hydrates the part the user interacts with first.
In development, `<StrictMode>` **renders components twice** and **runs effects twice** (mount, unmount, mount) to expose impure rendering and missing cleanups. Nothing is doubled in production.

A build-time tool (stable as **1.0** since October 2025) that **memoizes automatically**: it analyses components and caches values and JSX at a fine grain, so you rarely need `useMemo`, `useCallback` or `memo`. It relies on your code following the Rules of React.

React attaches **one listener per event type** to the root container and dispatches synthetic events through the component tree. Events from a portal bubble through the **React** tree, not the DOM tree.
Simplified fields of one fiber:

```jsx
{
  type: Counter,         // function, class or 'div'
  key: null,
  stateNode: null,       // DOM node for host fibers
  child, sibling, return,// tree links
  pendingProps, memoizedProps,
  memoizedState,         // hooks linked list
  updateQueue,
  flags,                 // Placement, Update, …
  lanes,                 // pending priorities
  alternate              // the other version
}
```

React keeps two trees: **current** (on screen) and **work-in-progress**. Each fiber points to its twin through `alternate`. Work happens on the work-in-progress tree; at commit React swaps the pointer, so the new tree becomes current in one step.

Rendering is a loop over units of work. `beginWork` renders a fiber and returns its child; when there is no child, `completeWork` finishes it and moves to the sibling or back up. In concurrent mode the loop checks `shouldYield()` between units.

- **Render phase**: asynchronous and interruptible, no side effects, may run several times
- **Commit phase**: synchronous, applies DOM mutations, then layout effects; passive effects (`useEffect`) are scheduled after paint

data.text: Lin Clark explains Fiber with drawings, React Conf 2017. *Meta Developers.*

- Stale closures
- Race conditions when fetching
- Missing cleanup
- Objects and functions in dependencies
- Effects that only sync state

- State is a snapshot
- Mutating instead of replacing
- Storing derived state
- Resetting state with a key

- Index keys on lists that move
- Components defined inside components
- `0 &&` renders "0"
- Memo broken by new objects
- Context re-rendering everything

- Hydration mismatches
- The client/server boundary
- Server Functions are public endpoints
- Error boundaries and async errors
Each topic opens into cards with the **problem**, a **fix**, and code. Most of these come up in code review and interviews.

An effect or callback **closes over** the values from the render that created it. This interval always sees `count = 0`, so the counter stops at 1. Fix: use an **updater function**, or `useEffectEvent` to read fresh values.
If `id` changes quickly, an older request can finish **last** and overwrite newer data. Ignore stale responses with a flag, or abort them.
Every subscription, timer and listener needs a cleanup, or it **leaks** and keeps firing after unmount. Strict Mode's double run in development makes a missing cleanup visible.

Dependencies are compared with `Object.is`. An object or function created during render is **new every time**, so the effect runs on every render. Move it inside the effect, or depend on primitive values.
Setting state in an effect from other state causes an **extra render** with a moment of stale UI. Compute it during render instead, and handle user actions in **event handlers**.
`useEffect` runs after paint, so measuring and repositioning there can show the wrong position for a frame. Measure in `useLayoutEffect`, which runs before the browser paints.
Calling the setter doesn't change the variable in the current render. Three `setCount(count + 1)` calls all use `0`, so the result is **1**. Use updaters to queue changes.

```jsx
function handleClick() {
  setCount(count + 1) // 0 + 1
  setCount(count + 1) // 0 + 1
  console.log(count)  // still 0
}

// Result 3 with updaters:
setCount((c) => c + 1)
setCount((c) => c + 1)
setCount((c) => c + 1)
```
React compares the old and new state with `Object.is`. Pushing into the same array keeps the **same reference**, so React may skip the render. Always create a new array or object.
Copying props into state means the copy goes **out of date** when the prop changes. Keep only the minimal state and compute the rest; store an **id** rather than a copy of the selected object.
State belongs to a **position in the tree**. Rendering the same component in the same place keeps its state, even for a different user. Give it a different `key` to start fresh.

data.label: Index keys on lists that move

data.text: With `key={index}`, inserting at the top shifts every key, so React gives the **wrong state** (input text, checkboxes) to the wrong row. Use a stable id from the data.
A component declared inside another is a **new type on every render**. React unmounts and remounts it each time: state is lost, inputs lose focus. Declare components at the top level.
`&&` returns its left side when it is falsy. `false`, `null` and `undefined` render nothing, but **0** is rendered as text.

`memo` skips a re-render only if **every prop is the same** (`Object.is`). An inline object, array or arrow function is new each time, so the memo never helps. Memoize those props, or let the React Compiler do it.

When a provider's value changes, **every** component that reads it re-renders. Passing a new object each render re-renders them all, every time. Memoize the value, or split rarely and often changing data into separate contexts.

During a concurrent render, a store outside React can change halfway, so different components show **different values** of the same data. `useSyncExternalStore` prevents this; state libraries use it internally.

The first client render must produce the **same HTML** as the server. `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `window` checks or locale formatting during render break this. Use `useId` for ids, render browser-only parts after mounting, or since **19.3** call `use(browser())` to skip server rendering for a component.

```jsx
import { use, Suspense } from 'react'
import { browser } from 'react-dom'

function TimeZone() {
  use(browser()) // suspends on the server
  return Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone
}

<Suspense fallback="…"><TimeZone /></Suspense>
```

- Server Components can't use state, effects or browser APIs
- `'use client'` marks a file as the **entry** to client code; everything it imports is client code too
- Props passed from server to client must be **serializable**: no functions except Server Functions, no class instances
- A client component can't import a server component, but can receive one as `children`

A `'use server'` function can be called by **anyone** with a POST request, not only by your form. Always **validate input and check authorisation** inside it. Keep React up to date: a critical remote-code-execution bug in Server Components was fixed in December 2025 (19.0.1, 19.1.2, 19.2.1).

An error boundary catches errors **during rendering** in its subtree and shows a fallback. It is still a **class** component. It does **not** catch errors in event handlers, timeouts or async code; handle those with try/catch.
Jordan Walke builds a prototype at Facebook, inspired by XHP. It powers the News Feed in 2011 and Instagram in 2012.
Released at **JSConf US**. Many developers dislike JSX at first; Pete Hunt's talk *Rethinking best practices* argues for it.
Facebook presents the **Flux** pattern for one-way data flow. Redux (2015) later becomes the most popular take on it.
Announced at React.js Conf: native iOS (later Android) apps with the same component model.
`react-dom` split out of `react`; **stateless function components**; refs to DOM nodes are the nodes themselves.
Version jump from 0.14 to 15. Initial render uses `document.createElement`; no more extra `<span>`s around text.
Zero-configuration starter that becomes the standard way to begin a project for years.
Core rewritten as **Fiber**. Components can return arrays and strings; **error boundaries**, **portals**, faster streaming SSR. React is relicensed under **MIT**.
New **Context API**, `createRef`, `forwardRef`, `<StrictMode>`, `getDerivedStateFromProps`; old lifecycles get the `UNSAFE_` prefix.
`React.memo`, `React.lazy` with `<Suspense>` for code splitting, `static contextType`.
**Hooks** ship, introduced at React Conf 2018. Function components can now have state and effects.
"No new features": gradual upgrades, events attached to the **root** instead of `document`, the new **JSX transform** (no `import React` needed).
First look at zero-bundle-size **React Server Components**, as research.

**Concurrent rendering** with `createRoot`; automatic batching; transitions (`useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`); streaming SSR with Suspense and selective hydration; `useId`, `useSyncExternalStore`.
New documentation site, teaching **function components and Hooks** first, with interactive examples.
Frameworks can adopt features early. Next.js 13.4 makes its App Router, built on Server Components, stable.
Open-sourced as experimental at React Conf 2024; beta in October 2024.

**Actions** and `useActionState`, `useOptimistic`, `useFormStatus`, `use()`; `<form action>`; `ref` as a prop; `<Context>` as provider; `<title>` and stylesheets anywhere; Server Components stable. Removed: `propTypes`, string refs, legacy context, `ReactDOM.render`.
Create React App is sunset; new apps should use a framework or a build tool such as **Vite**.
**Owner Stacks** for debugging (`captureOwnerStack`) and Suspense improvements.
`<Activity>` to hide UI and keep its state, `useEffectEvent`, `cacheSignal`, **Performance Tracks** in Chrome DevTools, partial pre-rendering.
**React Compiler 1.0** is stable, and the React Foundation is announced at React Conf 2025.
A critical remote-code-execution vulnerability in Server Components is fixed in 19.0.1, 19.1.2 and 19.2.1; more fixes follow on 11 December.
The **React Foundation** launches under the Linux Foundation, taking over governance from Meta.

`<ViewTransition>` and **Fragment refs** become stable; `use(browser())` opts a component out of server rendering; Trusted Types support; `<Context>` in Server Components. Patch **19.3.1** follows on 14 October.
Several components that work together and share state through a private context, like `<select>` and `<option>`.
For app-wide state without a library: a reducer holds the logic, and two contexts pass down the state and `dispatch` separately.

data.label: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context — react.dev

data.text: The older ways to share logic: a function prop that returns JSX (`render={data => …}`), or a function that wraps a component (`withRouter(Page)`). Custom hooks replaced most of them; you still meet them in older code and libraries.
`createPortal(children, domNode)` renders into a different DOM node, such as `document.body` for modals and tooltips, while staying in the same React tree for context and events.
Use the **React DevTools Profiler** and, since 19.2, React's **Performance Tracks** in Chrome DevTools. Test with a production build: development mode is much slower.

- **Move state down** into the component that uses it
- **Lift content up**: pass expensive parts as `children`, which don't re-render when the wrapper's state changes
`memo(Component)` skips re-rendering when props are equal; `useMemo` and `useCallback` keep values and functions stable. With the **React Compiler** this happens automatically.

- **Virtualise** long lists: render only visible rows (TanStack Virtual, react-window)
- Wrap slow, non-urgent updates in `startTransition`
- **Code-split** routes with `lazy()` and `<Suspense>`

1. **Local state** in the component that needs it
2. **Lifted** to the closest common parent
3. **Context** for widely used, rarely changing values
4. A **store** for complex shared client state
5. **URL** for anything you want shareable or bookmarkable

- **Server data**: TanStack Query, SWR, or your framework's loaders; caching, refetching and deduping are solved there
- **Client state**: Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai
- **Forms**: React 19 Actions, React Hook Form
Client-side rendering: the server sends an empty page and JavaScript builds the UI. Simple to host; slower first load and weaker SEO.
Server-side rendering: HTML is generated per request, then **hydrated**. Fast first paint; needs a server.
Static generation: HTML is rendered at **build time**. Fastest to serve; content is fixed until the next build.
Components that run **only on the server** (or at build time). Their code never reaches the browser; they can read files and databases directly.
An async Server Component fetches data and passes it to a Client Component, which handles interaction.
A `'use server'` function can be passed to `<form action>`. React submits the form, runs the function on the server and tracks the pending state; it even works before JavaScript loads.

The React team recommends a **framework** for new apps:
- **Next.js**: App Router built on Server Components
- **React Router v7**: framework mode (Remix merged into it)
- **Expo**: React Native apps for iOS, Android and web
- **TanStack Start**: full-stack, built on TanStack Router

For single-page apps, use a build tool: **Vite**, Parcel or Rsbuild. Create React App was deprecated in February 2025. You then choose routing (React Router, TanStack Router) and data fetching yourself.

**What is the virtual DOM?**
A tree of plain objects describing the UI. React compares the new tree with the old one (reconciliation) and applies only the differences to the real DOM.

**Why do lists need keys?**
Keys tell React which item is which between renders, so it can keep state with the right item and move DOM nodes instead of recreating them.

**Props vs state?**
Props are inputs from the parent and read-only. State is owned by the component, changes over time and triggers re-renders.

**Controlled vs uncontrolled?**
Controlled: React state holds the value (`value` + `onChange`). Uncontrolled: the DOM holds it, read with a ref or `FormData`.

**useEffect vs useLayoutEffect?**
`useEffect` runs after paint and doesn't block it. `useLayoutEffect` runs before paint, for measuring the DOM to avoid flicker.

**useMemo vs useCallback?**
`useMemo` caches the result of a function; `useCallback` caches the function itself. `useCallback(fn, d)` equals `useMemo(() => fn, d)`.

**Why can't hooks be conditional?**
React stores hooks by call order on the fiber. Skipping one shifts every later hook onto the wrong state.

**What causes a re-render?**
Its state changes, its parent re-renders, or a context it reads changes. Changed props alone don't; a parent render does.

**How do you stop needless re-renders?**
Move state down, pass children, split contexts, then `memo` with stable props, or the React Compiler. Measure with the Profiler first.

**Class lifecycles as hooks?**
mount → `useEffect(fn, [])`; update → `useEffect(fn, [deps])`; unmount → the effect's cleanup; `shouldComponentUpdate` → `memo`.

**What is Fiber?**
The reconciliation engine since React 16: work is split into units (fibers) so rendering can pause, resume and be prioritised.

**What are Server Components?**
Components that run only on the server, send no JavaScript to the client and can access data directly. Interactive parts are Client Components marked `'use client'`.
Short snippets about batching, snapshots and effect order. Open for the answers.
Common tasks: debounced search, fetch with abort, a todo list, a modal. Open for solutions.

**Tip**
Interviewers care about **why**: explain trade-offs, mention what you would measure, and say when you would *not* reach for an effect or a memo.

**Answer**: render Parent, render Child, **effect Child**, effect Parent. Rendering goes top-down, but effects run **children first**. In Strict Mode development you see each line twice.

Search as the user types, without a request per keystroke, ignoring stale responses.
Add, toggle and remove items with immutable updates and stable keys.
Renders into `document.body`, closes on Escape, and cleans up its listener.
An interval stored in a ref, with an updater so it never reads stale state.
